title: Praggnanandhaa Becomes First Indian to Win Grand Chess Tour After Stunning Comeback in St. Louis
excerpt: The 21-year-old Indian grandmaster overturned a six-point deficit on the final day, winning both rapid games against Fabiano Caruana before holding his nerve in blitz to seal a 15-13 victory and claim the $200,000 top prize.
body:
• R Praggnanandhaa defeated Fabiano Caruana 15-13 in the Grand Chess Tour Finals in St. Louis, becoming the first Indian player to win the prestigious series.
  • The 21-year-old erased a six-point deficit on the final day by winning both rapid games, then holding steady in blitz to secure the title.
  • Praggnanandhaa earned $200,000 for the Finals victory and $404,354 in total prize money across the 2026 Grand Chess Tour season.
  • Wesley So secured third place with an 18-12 blitz rout of Vincent Keymer, with the top three qualifying for the 2027 Tour.

R Praggnanandhaa pulled off one of the most dramatic comebacks in Grand Chess Tour history on Thursday, overcoming a six-point deficit against Fabiano Caruana on the final day of the GCT Finals to become the first Indian player to win the prestigious series.

The 21-year-old grandmaster's 15-13 aggregate victory in St. Louis capped a remarkable 2026 season that included victories at Norway Chess and the St. Louis Rapid & Blitz, earning him $404,354 in total Tour prize money.

Six Points Down, Two Rapid Wins Up

Caruana entered the final day with a commanding lead after winning the first classical game and forcing a draw in the second. The American grandmaster appeared poised to become the first player to win the GCT Finals in consecutive years.

Praggnanandhaa had other plans. In the first rapid game, his 5.Qd3 in the Ragozin Defense fractured Caruana's pawn structure early. As Caruana's clock dwindled to under three minutes, the pressure became unbearable and Praggnanandhaa converted the full point.

The second rapid game was equally decisive. Playing the black side of a Rossolimo Sicilian, Praggnanandhaa equalized comfortably before blasting open the center. Caruana's hasty 27.e5 left him close to lost, and the Indian grandmaster punished the error ruthlessly, winning again to take the overall lead.

"Honestly, I didn't think I had many chances today. It's not every day that you can get one win from Fabi, but to get two, it was important in the rapid."

— R Praggnanandhaa

A Blitz Section Full of Drama

With a two-point lead heading into the four-game blitz phase, Praggnanandhaa needed only to hold steady. The opening blitz game produced the day's first draw, though not without heart-stopping moments — Praggnanandhaa blundered with 25.Bb5, overlooking a tactic that should have given Caruana a winning position. Caruana, however, failed to find the winning continuation, and the game ended level.

Caruana struck back in the second blitz game, exploiting a time-scramble blunder to even the match score. But Praggnanandhaa reclaimed his advantage in game three, finding a decisive pawn break with just 13 seconds on his clock. The final game was enough to seal the deal — even Caruana's advantage from the Glek Variation evaporated after a premature pawn break, and Praggnanandhaa forced a perpetual check to clinch the title.

A Season for the Ages

The Grand Chess Tour title adds to what has been a transformative year for Praggnanandhaa. At Norway Chess in June, he won four consecutive classical games — including victories over world champion Gukesh Dommaraju, Magnus Carlsen, Alireza Firouzja, and Vincent Keymer — to claim his first classical super-tournament title. He followed that with a dominant wire-to-wire victory at the St. Louis Rapid & Blitz in August.

Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay felicitated the grandmaster in Chennai after his Norway Chess triumph, presenting him with a ₹50 lakh cash prize from the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu.

"It would have been nice to have it in the Candidates, but it's still nice to win tournaments like this. I consider the GCT second to the world championship, because of the tradition."

— R Praggnanandhaa

So Dominates Third-Place Match

Wesley So produced his own comeback in the third-place match against Vincent Keymer. After trailing by two points, So won the first rapid game and then took complete control in blitz, winning all four games to clinch an emphatic 18-12 victory. The performance guaranteed So a spot in next year's Tour along with Praggnanandhaa and Caruana.

The 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals featured a $450,000 prize pool across the knockout format, with matches consisting of two classical, two rapid, and four blitz games. GM Maurice Ashley called the Finals the most exciting in GCT history, with a nearly 70% rate of decisive games over the final three days.

Praggnanandhaa said he would like to rest for a week or two before the Chess Olympiad, which begins in less than a month.
nri_angle: Praggnanandhaa becomes the first Indian to win the Grand Chess Tour, adding to a transformative 2026 that has cemented India as a global chess powerhouse.
